title: After a year of failing to find one good AI trading strategy, I split $10,000 across 52 mediocre ones. Backtest vs reality.
author: LeastTangelo6022
selftext:
A few months ago I posted here about a year of vibe trading with AI. The short version: across about 20 strategy families, almost nothing survived honest validation (fees on, out-of-sample, deflated for the number of things I tried). A lot of you asked "ok, so what **do** you do then?"



This is what I tried next. Not a better strategy: more of them, uncorrelated.



**The setup**

\* 52 assets on Hyperliquid perps: crypto, plus stock and index perps, gold, silver and oil.

\* For each asset, I took the best published strategy I had access to: at least 100 trades and 36 months of history.

\* $10,000 split equally, so about $190 per strategy.

\* Every strategy trades only its own asset, with its own rules and its own stop.



**What the backtest said (36 months)**



\> +87.1%, Sharpe 2



That is the only real lesson in this post. **Correlation did more work than strategy quality**. A pile of boring 0.8s that don't overlap beats one "great" 2.0 that's secretly just long beta.



**Why you shouldn't believe that +87.1%**



\> Selection bias. I picked the best strategy per asset out of up to 52 candidates each. That alone inflates the backtest. I knew it going in.



\> Fees and funding. Turning them on took it from +87.1% to +72.4% (Sharpe 2.49 → 2.08). That's about 6 points over 36 months, a fifth of



Note: most of this window is paper / replay of signals after the strategies were published, not real fills.



\> 55 days, fully invested: the backtest expected +5.9% ± 5.3%. I got +1.8%. Below expectation, but inside 2 standard deviations. Way too short to conclude anything, but I'm not going to pretend it's a win.



\> The interesting stat: even at peak, only $3,740 of the $10,000 was used as margin. People see "idle capital" and want the bot to trade more. Some of that idle cash is the buffer that keeps you alive. More activity is not better capital management.



I put about $10k live on another 52-strategy version in mid-September. Too early to say anything; I'll post the numbers when it has 3 months.



**What I learned**



1. Stop asking AI "find me the best strategy." Ask "what is missing from what I already run?" A strategy with a worse standalone return can be the best addition if it trades when the others wait, or loses at different times.

2. A short is not automatically a hedge, and gold is not automatically diversification. Sizing and timing decide that, not the label.

3. Your account size changes your strategy. 

4. Judge the combined setup, never the sum of individual backtests.

5. The backtest is the most optimistic number you will ever see. 



Curious how others here handle this. Do you run one strategy you trust, or many you don't fully trust? And has anyone found a clean way to correct for selection bias when you pick "the best per asset"?

comments.author: LeastTangelo6022
comments.body: Since a few people DMed me last time: I build this on Trigr (trigr.xyz), where an agent can hold up to 52 strategies, one per asset, with a combined backtest. I connect it to Claude via MCP to do the assembly. It's in closed beta, so DM me if you want a code. Happy to answer questions about the method either way, no need to use it.

comments.author: Signal_Pace_7968
comments.body:
On the selection bias question, one simple way: do the same picking with fake strategies. For each asset make 52 versions with random entries (same stops, same holding time), pick the best one per asset like you did, and run the combined backtest. Whatever that shows is roughly what the picking alone gives you. Your number minus that is closer to the real edge.

Or pick the best per asset on the first 18 months and only judge them on the last 18.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: low correlation over 36 months is mostly calm-market correlation. on a liquidation day most of those perps fall together, the stock and index ones included. what does the pairwise look like on just the worst 20 days?

replies.author: LeastTangelo6022
replies.body:
Fair point, and you're probably right about the assets. 0.02 is a median over all days, and most days are calm. On a cascade day almost everything with crypto collateral gets hit, stock perps included since they trade 24/7.

Two things make the strategy legs behave differently from the assets though: on any given day a lot of legs are flat (waiting for their setup), and some are short. So "assets fall together" doesn't automatically mean "legs lose together". Each leg also has its own stop. For what it's worth, the worst drawdown over the whole window was −5.7%, and the window includes last October's liquidation cascade.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: the legs can decorrelate even when the collateral doesn't. shared margin is still the weak link though: on a cascade day the strategies don't all need to lose, one forced close on shared collateral can drag the others down with it.

comments.author: Maleficent-Success-6
comments.body:
I'm running a 90-day paper experiment at TIYlab with 49 virtual portfolios, and one thing I've noticed is how misleading raw P&L comparisons can be when exposure differs.

Have you compared your 52-strategy portfolio against a much simpler portfolio with roughly the same exposure? I'd be curious how much of the improvement comes from diversification alone.

comments.author: Bergodrake
comments.body: We’ve taken a somewhat similar approach with Trigol.io: hundreds of ML models generating short-term stock signals, with the real challenge being how to select and combine them rather than finding one perfect model. Diversification helps, but we’ve found that filtering signals and managing exposure matter just as much. Very interesting experiment!

comments.author: Hour-Muffin2844
comments.body: The first point is cool. Gonna use it

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Praise for the honesty here, the point that correlation did more work than strategy quality is well put. For selection bias, one clean fix is to run the same "pick the best per asset" step on randomly generated strategies, so you can see what the best of N candidates looks like by luck alone, and then judge your picks against that. Also choose the picks using one period and judge them only on a later one they never touched, even if that means a shorter test. Since the replay after publication isn't real fills, the live three months is the number that will count. Cymetica's Backtest Labs is one place to check strategies against history with fees included.

comments.author: Obviously_not_maayan
comments.body: This sound like BS sorry, combining a mix of C grade strategies and expecting they compliment each other just on diversity doesn't make sense to me, it could as easily flip to the other side. did you do out of time validation? Or this 36 month results are in sample? Out of time validation should help cancel the selection bias, but I'm suspecting it's not going to pass. Sorry if this brutal just seems like a bad idea to me.
